tldr: We propose CoRe, a training-free inference-time framework that recovers VLA models without additional fine-tuning or failure data. Using geometrically synthesized 'what-if' visual observations, it simulates recovery trajectories entirely in the mind of the VLA, safely rejoining the task with only minimal physical rearrangements.
hero_caption: Overview of the CoRe framework. Upon detecting an out-of-distribution (OOD) state, online execution of the VLA is paused, and a counterfactual rollout is performed from a recent viable anchor in imagination to determine the rejoin state $c^*$ and the minimal restoration set $S^*$. Physical motions occur only during final tidying and rejoining.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robotic actions directly from camera images and natural language, showing remarkable promise. However, they remain notoriously fragile when faced with mid-episode instruction changes or online disruptions like collisions and dropped objects. Because VLAs are trained exclusively on successful, clean demonstrations, they cannot self-recover once an unexpected event pushes them out of distribution (OOD).

Existing countermeasures typically rely on collecting failure data to retrain the policy, or delegating corrective behaviors to external LLM agents. Both approaches entail heavy data collection costs and risk dangerous physical trial-and-error in the real world. To avoid this, the authors asked: could we recover a frozen policy at inference time without any retraining? Their answer is counterfactual continuation. When an anomaly occurs, the system virtually rewinds to a safe, recent checkpoint and simulates how the VLA should proceed toward the current goal using visual observations synthesized geometrically from RGB-D history. To rejoin this imagined trajectory, only the minimal set of objects that actually interfere with the task are physically rearranged.

Evaluations across simulators (ManiSkill, robosuite) and a real-world xArm6 under diverse disruptions—such as instruction switches, collisions, and dropped or tipped objects—demonstrated up to an 85.0 percentage point improvement in success rates, reaching near-nominal levels while reducing physical restoration operations by 42.2%, all without any policy fine-tuning.
contributions: Proposed CoRe, a training-free framework that recovers a frozen VLA at inference time without failure data or external reasoning agents.

Demonstrated that virtual VLA rollouts function effectively through lightweight geometric synthesis combining RGB-D history and forward kinematics (FK), avoiding heavy world models or privileged simulator states.
Established a probe-based minimal restoration method that filters down to only the objects required to rejoin the task, substantially reducing unnecessary physical resets.

sections.heading: Why Do VLAs Fail to Recover Once Off-Track?
sections.summary: Trained only on successful demonstrations, VLAs are fragile to mid-episode instruction switches and physical disturbances. To resolve the limitations of failure retraining and external agents, CoRe performs counterfactual imagination purely at inference time to plan safe recoveries.
sections.details:
VLA models are attracting widespread attention for their generalist ability to execute diverse robot tasks from text instructions. However, because training data almost universally consists of smooth, successful forward-progress trajectories, VLAs struggle when the robot drifts off course, objects are shifted, or the user changes the prompt mid-episode (language switching). In closed-loop execution, small errors compound rapidly into catastrophic task failure.

Prior efforts to address this challenge fall into two main categories. The first collects failure-recovery data via human interventions or simulation, fine-tuning or optimizing preferences on top of the policy. This requires laborious data collection and forces retraining whenever new failure modes appear. The second deploys external LLMs, VLMs, or auxiliary modules as monitors to diagnose failures and emit corrective actions. However, this introduces substantial inference overhead and shifts reliability onto whether the external module can produce feasible, precise actions. Furthermore, simple physical rollbacks to past checkpoints wipe out whatever task progress was already achieved.

The authors introduce CoRe (Counterfactual Realignment), a training-free framework designed to rescue existing frozen VLAs. Its core insight is to 'replay counterfactually in imagination.' When an anomaly is detected, CoRe locates a recent viable frame (anchor) that preserves completed progress, and rolls out how the VLA would proceed toward the updated goal using geometrically synthesized observations. The robot and environment are then minimally realigned to rejoin this imagined continuation. By completing planning safely in imagination, CoRe eliminates dangerous physical trial-and-error on the robot.

captions.F2: The complete CoRe pipeline. When an anomaly (OOD) is detected during physical execution (top), control switches to virtual planning (bottom). Following anchor identification, rollout via synthesized observations, and probe-based selection of minimal objects, physical restoration and rejoining are executed before returning control to the VLA.

sections.heading: A Third Way Beyond Policy Retraining and External Agents
sections.summary: Existing work focuses on failure-conditioned retraining or external LLM supervisors, which suffer from high cost and questionable reliability. CoRe detects anomalies directly from VLA latent features and completes the entire recovery pipeline without modifying policy weights or relying on auxiliary models.
sections.details:
Recent VLA architectures range from autoregressive models predicting tokenized actions alongside language, to diffusion models and flow-matching policies that output continuous action chunks at high frequencies. Yet none of these designs possess intrinsic self-recovery mechanisms.

Prior literature on failure detection and recovery splits into two directions:
- Failure-conditioned policy training: Gathering perturbation-injected trajectories or failure rollouts to retrain policies using behavioral cloning or reinforcement learning. This imposes heavy data-collection burdens and generalizes poorly to unseen failures.
- Delegation to external modules: Employing LLMs/VLMs for diagnosis or training residual policies to adjust actions online. These approaches suffer from runtime overhead and depend entirely on the external module's accuracy.

Meanwhile, recent work shows that internal latent features of a VLA can lightweightly distinguish success from failure trajectories. CoRe builds upon this insight, going beyond mere detection to construct the entire recovery pipeline—from anchor identification and counterfactual planning to minimal physical realignment—without policy retraining or external inference agents.

sections.heading: Imagining in the Mind, Tidying Only What Matters
sections.summary: CoRe operates in five stages: (1) latent-based OOD detection, (2) progress-preserving anchoring, (3) virtual rollout via synthesized images, (4) probe-based minimal restoration, and (5) physical realignment and handoff.
sections.details:
Mathematically, CoRe solves an inference-time optimization problem: find a rejoin state $c^*=(q^*, p^*)$—comprising robot joint configuration $q^*$ and scene layout $p^*$—that returns the VLA to its nominal distribution under the new instruction $\ell'$ while preserving achieved task progress $\mathcal{P}(c)$ and minimizing physical object manipulation $|\mathcal{R}(c)|$. It proceeds in five concrete steps:

- Suffix OOD Detection: The system monitors the action-expert suffix latent features right before the VLA action head. By tracking the Mahalanobis distance $s_t$ calibrated on nominal successful rollouts, an anomaly is flagged if $s_t$ exceeds a threshold $\tau_k$ for consecutive steps. No classifier training is needed, and calibration requires only normal execution data.
- Phase-Aware Recovery Anchoring: Upon detection, execution history is rewound to locate a viable anchor frame. CoRe identifies the step just before the action divergence $d_t$ between old and new instructions crosses a threshold $\delta$. Crucially, it selects a stable frame where the gripper is empty and in free space, avoiding moments mid-grasp or when objects are moving.
- Counterfactual Rollout via Geometric Synthesis: Starting from the anchor, the frozen VLA rolls out candidate actions under the new instruction $\ell'$ in imagination. Remarkably, without any neural world model, observations are synthesized geometrically (Figure F3) from historical RGB-D voxels combined with robot forward kinematics (FK). The virtual rollout runs until a gripper-to-object proximity threshold $d_{\text{prox}}$ is reached, setting this safe free-space pose as the rejoin state $c^*$.
- Probe-Based Minimal Restoration: Not every disturbed object needs to return to its original pose. Objects unrelated to the task can be safely ignored. For non-target objects outside the goal area, candidate subsets $S$ are tested through virtual rollouts (probes). CoRe selects the smallest subset $S^*$ whose resulting arm trajectory differs from a fully restored reference by less than a tolerance $\epsilon$, measured by $d_{\text{arm}}(S)$.
- Physical Realignment and Handoff: Only after planning finishes does the physical robot move. Standard pick-and-place motions restore only the selected minimal objects in $S^*$, the arm moves to rejoin configuration $q^*$, and closed-loop control is returned to the VLA.

captions.F3: Examples of geometrically synthesized observations. In both exocentric and egocentric views, the pipeline projects past voxel history, renders the arm via forward kinematics (FK), and inpaints missing background regions to produce clean visual inputs for the VLA.

sections.heading: Dramatic Recovery Performance Across Simulators and Real Hardware
sections.summary: Evaluated on simulators and a real xArm6 under instruction switches and physical disturbances, CoRe improved success rates by up to 85 percentage points over collapsing baselines while significantly cutting physical restoration operations.
sections.details:
CoRe was rigorously tested across three benchmark environments: 'LangSwitch' for instruction changes, 'LIBERO-Long with Perturbation' for physical disturbances, and a real-world robot setup.

- Experimental Setup:
  - LangSwitch (ManiSkill, xArm6): Involves five skills on a tabletop (picking, placing, pushing, stacking). Evaluated across three instruction-change categories: Re-grounding (target changes), Re-skilling (skill changes), and Conflict (goal contradicts previous action) (Figure F4).
  - LIBERO-Long (robosuite, Franka Panda): Covers 10 long-horizon tasks subjected to four physical disruption types: Arm Collision, Grasp Failure, Object Displace, and Object Tip (Figure F5), injected at early, middle, or late task stages.
  - Real Robot Setup (xArm6, two RealSense D435i cameras): Using a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone, tested on three language-switch and two physical disruption scenarios (Arm Collision and Scene Rearrangement by a human) (Figure F7).

- Key Results:
  - In LangSwitch, the unassisted baseline collapsed to 18.3–35.5% success, whereas CoRe boosted rates to 82.6–92.7%, showing strong resilience even under conflicting instructions.
  - In LIBERO-Long, baseline success ranged from 12.8% to 43.5%, while CoRe achieved 69.8–88.2%, displaying high robustness regardless of perturbation timing.
  - In real-world trials (Figure F9), the baseline achieved at most 9/20 successes (and only 1/20 on Re-skilling and Conflict), while CoRe consistently reached 17–19/20 (85–95%) success across all disruption types.

- Ablation and In-Depth Analysis:
  - Virtual Rollout Accuracy: Comparing synthesized rollouts against ground-truth execution revealed a median end-effector trajectory deviation of only 0.36 to 3.28 cm, well within the contact margin (2–8 cm).
  - Minimal Restoration Efficiency (Figure F10): In the real-world Scene Rearrangement setting where all three objects were displaced, CoRe restored an average of just 1.15 objects (42%), completing the task while leaving 58% untouched.
  - Timing and Safety: Virtual planning on real hardware required a median of only 9.7 seconds. Because physically moving an object takes 46.6 seconds, eliminating redundant manipulations saved 33 to 76 seconds per recovery. Furthermore, while the baseline suffered 21% collisions or E-stops, CoRe stops virtual rollouts at pre-contact safety margins, dramatically improving physical safety.

sections.heading: A New Paradigm of Imagined Recovery
sections.summary: CoRe presents a training-free framework that recovers VLAs using counterfactual imagination and minimal physical intervention. It achieves near-nominal task success and cuts physical resets across both simulation and real hardware.
sections.details:
Departing from the conventional wisdom of collecting failure datasets or delegating control to massive external LLMs, CoRe demonstrates an elegant inference-time alternative: eliciting the latent capabilities already present in a frozen VLA through geometrically synthesized imagination.

Extensive benchmarks and real-world experiments confirm that CoRe restores policy performance to near-nominal levels under sudden instruction shifts and severe physical disruptions, without any fine-tuning. Its probe-based mechanism cuts unnecessary resets, saving operational time and safeguarding physical hardware. This work represents a promising pioneer in applying inference-time computation to robotic failure recovery.

sections.heading: Appendix: Real-World Implementation and Hyperparameter Practicalities
sections.summary: Details on the real-robot perception pipeline, geometric observation synthesis techniques, and policy handoff strategies across different VLA backbones ($\pi_0$, GR00T, X-VLA).
sections.details:
The technical appendix provides critical implementation details for replicating CoRe:

- Real-Robot Perception Pipeline: Object detection is handled by Grounding-DINO and segmentation by SAM2. The robot's own arm is masked out using forward kinematics on joint angles followed by a 9px dilation, enabling clean point cloud and voxel maintenance without privileged simulation states.
- Observation Synthesis Practicalities: A local voxel grid with 2 mm resolution is maintained over time. Missing background regions are filled using past background voxels and inpainting (LaMa for large gaps, Telea for small ones). In the LIBERO simulator, headlight intensity was calibrated to eliminate lighting discrepancies with the external renderer.
- Handoff to Policy: For action-chunking architectures ($\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, GR00T), when a virtual rollout terminates mid-chunk, only the unexecuted remainder of the chunk is commanded to the real robot, preventing double execution. For models like X-VLA that output 30 absolute end-effector waypoints, open-loop execution is longer; here, the proximity margin is expanded to 15 cm, and the robot rejoins at the waypoint closest to its rearranged arm configuration.
- Sensitivity of Anchoring: Ablations show that setting the anchor divergence threshold $\delta$ too loosely causes the policy to attempt recovery from states where it has already locked onto the wrong object, dropping success rates steeply from 91.1% to 36.7%. Timely, phase-aware anchoring is crucial for robust recovery.

takeaways: Recovering VLAs does not strictly require failure data fine-tuning or large external LLMs; inference-time virtual simulations (counterfactual rollouts) can effectively substitute for them.
Without training heavy neural world models, simple geometric voxel synthesis from RGB-D history and forward kinematics (FK) produces visual observations convincing enough for frozen VLAs.
Virtual probing identifies the minimal subset of objects that truly affect recovery, significantly reducing redundant physical resets and collision risks.
Tracking the Mahalanobis distance of action-expert suffix latents provides an accurate, lightweight anomaly detector calibrated purely on nominal success data.
limitations: Because counterfactual rollouts rely on forward kinematics rather than dynamic physics simulation, they cannot model complex contact interactions, requiring virtual foresight to terminate strictly before contact.
Observation synthesis relies on the quality of RGB-D depth data and 2D segmentation masks (e.g., SAM2), making it vulnerable to heavy occlusions, transparent materials, or highly reflective surfaces.
Physical rearrangement depends on standard pick-and-place motion planners, limiting recovery when displaced objects end up in configurations that cannot be stably grasped.
